title: Steam, Iron and Endless Paper
summary: For 350 years, printers pulled heavy wooden presses by hand. Then came presses made of iron, then presses driven by roaring steam engines, and finally giant spinning machines fed by rolls of paper as long as a road. Paper itself got cheaper too, once people learned to make it from trees instead of old rags.

sections.heading: A Press Made of Iron
paragraphs: Imagine walking into a London print shop in the year 1799. It would look surprisingly like Gutenberg's workshop in Mainz more than three centuries earlier. The press is a tall wooden frame, held together with pegs and bolts. A pressman grabs the long bar, leans back with his whole body and pulls, and a wooden screw lowers a flat plate called the platen onto the paper and the inked type. Then he lets go, the platen lifts, and his partner peels off the sheet. Pull, lift, peel, repeat, all day long.

The wooden hand press had served the world well, but it had real weaknesses. Wood bends and warps, so the pressure across the page was never perfectly even. Most wooden presses had a platen only about half the size of a big sheet, so the pressman had to slide the type under and pull twice to print one side of a large page. It was exhausting work, and it set a hard speed limit on how much could be printed.

Around 1800 an English nobleman decided to fix this. Charles Stanhope, the 3rd Earl Stanhope (1753–1816), was a politician who loved science and gadgets. He experimented with steamboats, canal locks, a fireproofing method and even calculating machines. His most famous invention was the Stanhope press, usually described as the first printing press made entirely of iron.

Iron changed everything about the press. A cast-iron frame did not bend, so the platen could press evenly across the whole page. Because iron is so strong, the platen could be made big enough to print a full large sheet in one pull instead of two. Stanhope also added a clever system of levers linked to the screw. As the pressman pulled the bar, the levers gave him more and more pushing force right at the end of the pull, just when the platen touched the paper. That meant crisp, dark printing without a pressman wearing himself out.

Even so, the Stanhope press was still a hand press. A crew could make roughly 200 pulls an hour, which is about one impression every 18 seconds. A newspaper printed on both sides needed two pulls per sheet, so 200 pulls produced only about 100 finished copies. For a big city paper that wanted thousands of copies each morning, that was hopeless.

Other inventors quickly joined the race. In America, George Clymer of Philadelphia designed the Columbian press in the 1810s, often called the first all-metal press made in the United States. It is easy to recognize in museums because a cast-iron eagle sits on top, acting as a counterweight that lifts the platen back up. Later came the Albion press in England and the Washington press in America. These iron hand presses were so tough that many still work today in art studios and printing museums. But to really speed things up, someone would have to take the human arm out of the job altogether.

sections.heading: Friedrich Koenig and the Steam Press
paragraphs: That someone was Friedrich Koenig, a German printer and inventor born in 1774. Koenig had been dreaming about a machine press since his early years in the trade. Few people in Germany wanted to pay for his experiments, so in November 1806 he moved to London, where the Industrial Revolution was in full swing and steam engines were already pumping water from mines and turning machines in cotton mills.

In London Koenig teamed up with Andreas Bauer, a skilled German precision mechanic who had trained as a watchmaker, and with a London book printer named Thomas Bensley, who helped pay for the work. Koenig received a British patent for a printing machine in 1810, and his first trial of a working machine took place in April 1812.

Koenig's great idea was to stop squeezing the paper with a flat platen. Instead, the type lay on a flat bed that slid back and forth like a drawer. The paper was wrapped around a big turning cylinder. As the bed slid underneath, the cylinder rolled over the type, pressing the paper against it one narrow strip at a time, the way you might roll a rolling pin across dough. Because only a thin line of the cylinder touched the type at any moment, it needed far less force than pressing a whole page at once.

Koenig also got rid of the leather ink balls that printers had dabbed on type for centuries. In his machine, a set of rollers automatically picked up ink and spread it evenly over the type each time the bed passed. And instead of a strong pressman, the power came from a steam engine. Workers still had to feed each blank sheet in and take each printed sheet out by hand, but the hard, repetitive labour was now done by the engine.

Among the people invited to see Koenig's machines was John Walter II, the owner of The Times of London, one of the most important newspapers in Britain. Walter had a problem: the more readers wanted his paper, the more hand presses and pressmen he needed, and still the paper came out late. He ordered two of Koenig's machines.

According to the story told afterwards, Walter worried that his pressmen would be furious, or even try to wreck the machines, because they would fear losing their jobs. So the new presses were installed quietly in a separate building. Early on the morning of 29 November 1814, the pressmen were told to wait for important news from abroad. Then Walter walked in and announced that the paper had already been printed, by steam. That day's issue proudly told readers they were holding a newspaper printed by machine, which the paper described as the biggest improvement in printing since the art was first invented.

The numbers explain the excitement. Koenig's steam press could print about 1,100 sheets an hour, several times faster than a hand press. Koenig and Bauer soon built a double-cylinder machine that printed two sheets at once, and then a perfecting machine that printed both sides of a sheet in a single pass.

sections.heading: From London to a Monastery in Germany
paragraphs: Success did not make Koenig's life easy. He quarrelled with Thomas Bensley, who Koenig believed wanted to control the machine for himself. In August 1817 Koenig gave up on England and returned to Germany. Together with Bauer he set up a factory in an empty old monastery at Oberzell, near the city of Würzburg in Bavaria. The firm they founded, Koenig and Bauer, still builds printing presses today, more than two hundred years later, making it one of the oldest press makers in the world.

Koenig died in 1833, but his cylinder idea lived on everywhere. In Britain, engineers such as Augustus Applegath and Edward Cowper improved the machines for The Times, adding more cylinders and faster inking. In America, a press maker named Isaac Adams built a powered platen press that became popular for printing books. By the 1830s, steam presses were humming in print shops across Europe and North America.

It is worth noticing something important here. The steam press did not appear out of nowhere. It combined the old ideas of movable type and ink with brand-new ideas from the Industrial Revolution: precise iron parts made in machine shops, steam engines, gears and belts. Inventions almost always grow this way, by joining older ideas in new combinations. Gutenberg did it with the screw press in the 1400s, and Koenig did it with the steam engine in the 1800s.

There was also a business lesson. Historians point out that Koenig's machine was a success at The Times partly because almost no other publication of the time printed enough copies to justify such an expensive machine. A small-town printer making a few hundred posters a week did not need a steam monster. A huge daily newspaper did. As cities grew and more people learned to read, more and more printers found themselves in that second group.

sections.heading: Spinning Cylinders: Hoe's Lightning Press
paragraphs: Koenig's press still had a slow part: the heavy bed of type sliding back and forth. Every time it reached the end, it had to stop, reverse and come back, wasting time and shaking the machine. What if the type itself could spin, round and round, without ever stopping?

In New York, the Hoe family ran a company that built presses. Robert Hoe had started the business in 1805, making wood and iron machinery. His son Richard March Hoe (1812–1886) developed a rotary press in the 1840s, received a US patent for it in 1847, and put it into commercial use that same year. Fair credit matters here: an American inventor named Josiah Warren had shown a rotary press design back in 1832 but chose not to patent it. Hoe turned the idea into a practical, money-making machine.

In Hoe's press, the type for a page was locked onto a huge central cylinder that turned continuously. The pieces of type were held in special wedge-shaped frames so they would not fly off as the cylinder spun. Around this big drum stood several smaller impression cylinders, sometimes as many as ten, each with its own worker feeding in sheets of paper. With every turn of the giant drum, each small cylinder printed a sheet. People called it the Lightning Press, and the name fit. Each feeder could produce about 2,000 one-sided sheets an hour, so a ten-feeder machine could make around 20,000.
These monsters were big, noisy and expensive, often filling a whole room. But a newspaper with a large circulation could finally print its morning edition in a few hours instead of all night.

There was one more clever trick that made rotary printing practical. Instead of putting precious, fragile type on the cylinder, printers learned to make a copy of the whole page called a stereotype. Workers pressed a thick sheet of papier-mâché-like material onto the locked-up page of type to make a mould, bent the mould into a curve, and poured molten metal into it. Out came a solid, curved metal plate of the whole page that fitted neatly onto a cylinder. Stereotyping developed during the 1840s and became widespread in the 1860s. It protected the type from wear, freed the type for the next job, and let a newspaper cast several identical plates so that several presses could print the same page at once. Hoe's company began using stereotype plates in its presses in 1861, and newspapers kept using them until the 1970s.

sections.heading: The Endless Web, and the Price Bullock Paid
paragraphs: Even the Lightning Press needed people to feed in one sheet of paper at a time. The next leap was to stop using sheets altogether and feed the press from a giant roll of paper, which printers call a web.

William Bullock was born in 1813 in Greenville, New York. He had worked as a machinist and iron-founder, run his own machine shop, and even edited a newspaper in Philadelphia, and he had been tinkering with self-feeding presses since the 1850s. On 14 April 1863 he received US patent number 38,200 for a printing press that used a continuous web of paper. Working with papermakers, he had the paper made in long rolls, and by around 1865 his presses were running on them.

Here is how a web press works. A huge roll of paper sits at one end, mounted on an axle. The paper unrolls and threads through the machine like a ribbon. It passes between cylinders that print one side, then between more cylinders that print the other side, so the sheet is printed on both sides in one pass. Printers call this perfecting. Finally, a sharp knife on a turning cylinder cuts the ribbon into separate sheets. Nobody has to feed paper by hand. The press just keeps eating paper as fast as the roll can turn.

Bullock's press could print up to about 12,000 sheets an hour, and later improvements pushed it to as many as 30,000. The New-York Tribune reported that early Bullock presses were turning out roughly 8,000 to 10,000 copies an hour.

Sadly, Bullock's own invention led to his death. On 3 April 1867 he was adjusting one of his new presses being installed at the Philadelphia Public Ledger newspaper. He tried to kick a driving belt back onto a pulley, and his leg was caught and crushed in the machinery. The wound became badly infected, and on 12 April 1867 he died during an operation to remove the leg. In those days before modern antibiotics, infections from injuries were often deadly. His story is a reminder that the early factories and print rooms were dangerous places, full of fast belts and gears with no safety guards.

Others carried the web press forward. Hoe's company built a web perfecting press that the New-York Tribune used from 1875, turning out about 14,000 complete copies an hour. Machines were added that folded the newspapers automatically as they came off the press. By the late 1800s, the biggest newspaper presses could print tens of thousands of sheets an hour. Remember the Stanhope press, at about 200 pulls an hour? In less than a hundred years, printing speed had multiplied by more than a hundred.

sections.heading: A Machine That Makes Endless Paper
paragraphs: All these fast presses had a very hungry appetite. A press that printed tens of thousands of sheets an hour needed mountains of paper, and a web press needed paper in long, unbroken rolls. But for most of history, paper had been made one sheet at a time by hand.

In a traditional paper mill, a worker called a vatman dipped a wire mould into a tub of watery pulp, lifted it out, and shook it gently so the fibers spread and tangled. Another worker flipped the wet sheet onto a piece of felt. Stacks of sheets were squeezed in a press and hung up to dry. Skilled teams worked fast, but each sheet could never be bigger than the mould, and there was a limit to how many sheets people could make in a day.

The solution came from France. Louis-Nicolas Robert (1761–1828) worked at a paper mill at Essonnes, south of Paris, owned by the Didot family. In 1799 Robert was granted a French patent for a machine that made paper in one continuous strip. In his machine, pulp flowed onto an endless belt of woven wire mesh that moved along like a conveyor belt. Water drained through the mesh, and the fibers knitted into a long wet sheet.

Robert and his employer, Saint-Léger Didot, argued over who owned the invention. France was in turmoil after the Revolution, so Didot sent his English brother-in-law, John Gamble, to Britain to find support. Gamble met two London stationers, the brothers Henry and Sealy Fourdrinier, who agreed to pay for the development. They hired a talented engineer named Bryan Donkin. In 1803 an improved machine was installed at Frogmore Mill in Apsley, Hertfordshire, and another followed in 1804.

The Fourdrinier brothers spent huge sums on the project and ended up going bankrupt, but their name stuck. Today a paper machine of this type is still called a Fourdrinier machine. Modern ones follow the same basic plan as the early ones, in much bigger form. At the wet end, a watery mixture of fibers that is almost all water sprays onto a fast-moving wire mesh. Water drains away and the fibers lock together. Next, the wet sheet passes through presses that squeeze out more water. Then it winds around dozens of steam-heated drying cylinders. Finally, polished rollers called calenders smooth it, and the finished paper is wound onto a giant reel.

The science is the same as in the paper Cai Lun's workers made in China nearly 1,700 years earlier: tangled plant fibers, held together by hydrogen bonds as they dry. The difference is speed and size. Modern paper machines can be longer than a football field and produce a sheet of paper several meters wide, moving faster than a car on a city street.

sections.heading: Paper from Trees: Friedrich Gottlob Keller
paragraphs: Machines solved the problem of making paper fast, but not the problem of what to make it from. European paper had been made mostly from old linen and cotton rags. Rag collectors went from door to door buying old clothes and cloth scraps. As printing exploded in the 1800s, there simply were not enough rags in the world to feed all the paper machines. Papermakers searched for something else: straw, grasses, even other plants.

The answer was standing all around them in forests. More than a century earlier, in 1719, the French scientist René-Antoine Ferchault de Réaumur had noticed that wasps build their papery nests by chewing wood into a pulp, and he suggested humans might make paper from wood too. For a long time, nobody managed to do it on a practical scale.

Friedrich Gottlob Keller was born on 27 June 1816 in Hainichen, in the Kingdom of Saxony in Germany. His father was a weaver, and young Friedrich worked in the family trade, though he much preferred machines. In 1841 he wrote an idea in his notebook, which he called his idea book: a machine to grind wood into fibers. Inspired partly by Réaumur's suggestion, he spent the next few years working on it. By 1844 he had built a grinder that held a piece of wood against a turning, wet grindstone. The stone tore the wood into tiny fibers, which mixed with water into a pulp. Keller made paper from this ground wood pulp.

In the summer of 1844 Keller sent a sample to the government of Saxony, hoping for money to build a better grinder. He got none. He did not have the money to develop the idea himself, so he sold his invention to a paper manufacturer named Heinrich Voelter for a small sum. A patent was granted in August 1845 in both their names, but in 1852 Keller could not pay his share to renew it, and Voelter became the only owner. Voelter and the engineer Johann Matthäus Voith turned Keller's idea into an industry. Keller himself earned no royalties. Later in life, German paper makers collected money to thank him, and he lived out his years in the town of Krippen, where he died in 1895.

Fair credit, again: in the same years, a man named Charles Fenerty in Nova Scotia, Canada, also made paper from wood pulp and announced his discovery in 1844, apparently without knowing about Keller. Like many inventions, wood pulp paper was found by more than one person at nearly the same time.

Ground wood pulp made weak paper on its own, so it was often mixed with stronger fibers. Later in the 1800s, chemists found ways to cook wood chips in chemicals to free the fibers more completely, making stronger paper. Together, these methods made paper astonishingly cheap. Trees, unlike rags, could be grown in enormous numbers. Cheap wood-pulp paper had a hidden flaw, though: much of it was acidic and slowly turned yellow and brittle. That problem, and what libraries do about it, is a story for later in this Deep Dive.

sections.heading: Penny Papers, Pickwick and the Reading Explosion
paragraphs: Put fast steam presses, endless paper and cheap wood pulp together, and something remarkable happens: reading becomes affordable for almost everyone.

In the early 1800s, an American newspaper typically cost about six cents, a lot of money for a working family. In September 1833, a young New York printer named Benjamin Day launched The Sun and sold it for just one cent. His paper promised to give everyone all the news of the day at a price anyone could pay. Day hired boys to sell papers on street corners, shouting the headlines, and the newsboy became a famous sight in cities. Two years later James Gordon Bennett started the New York Herald, packed with local news, crime reports, interviews and a page about money. These cheap, lively papers became known as the penny press, and their huge sales only made sense because steam presses could print so many copies so quickly.

In Britain, magazines took off too. Charles Knight's Penny Magazine, started in 1832, sold more than 200,000 copies in its first year, offering cheap articles about science, history and art to working people.

Novels changed shape as well. In April 1836 a young writer named Charles Dickens began publishing The Pickwick Papers not as a single expensive book but in monthly parts, each costing a shilling. Sales started small, but once Dickens introduced the funny servant Sam Weller, they soared. By the final double issue in November 1837, the parts were selling about 40,000 copies, and the publishers had to keep reprinting the early parts. Dickens published most of his later novels as serials in parts or in magazines too. Readers waited eagerly for each new installment, a bit like waiting for the next episode of a TV series today.

Cheap printing also transformed schools. Textbooks, readers and spelling books could be printed by the hundreds of thousands. In the United States, the McGuffey Readers, first published in the 1830s, taught generations of children to read and sold many millions of copies. As more countries introduced public schooling for all children, such as Britain's Education Act of 1870, millions of new readers wanted newspapers, magazines and books. Railways, another steam-age invention, carried bundles of newspapers from city presses to towns far away, often by the next morning.

So by 1880 the world of print looked completely different from 1800. Presses were made of iron and steel, driven by steam, fed by rolls of paper made by machines from trees. A single big-city newspaper could print more copies in one night than a fifteenth-century printer might make in years.

But there was still a bottleneck hiding in plain sight. Before any page reached those roaring machines, a compositor had to stand at a type case and set it, picking up every single letter with his fingers, just as in Gutenberg's day. And pictures were still a struggle: a photograph could not simply be dropped onto a printed page. Presses were now lightning fast, but setting the type was still done by hand, one letter at a time, and pictures were hard to print. The next great inventors would set out to solve both problems.

deepDive: Why did printing speed jump so dramatically in the 1800s? Engineers often explain it with two ideas: reciprocating versus rotary motion, and batch versus continuous feeding. A flat-bed press, even Koenig's, is reciprocating: the bed must accelerate, travel, stop and reverse. Every reversal wastes time and puts heavy stress on the machine, so there is a practical speed limit. A rotary press removes the stop-and-reverse cycle entirely, because a cylinder can turn at a steady speed forever. Contact between a cylinder and the paper is also a narrow line rather than a whole page, so much less total force is needed for a sharp impression. The second idea, continuous feeding, removed the human from the loop. Even a very skilled feeder can only place so many sheets per minute onto a cylinder. Bullock's web, and Hoe's later web perfecting presses, replaced that human rate limit with the speed at which a reel of paper can unwind, which is limited mainly by how strong wet ink and paper are and how fast the cutting and folding can keep up. The numbers tell the story: roughly 200 pulls an hour for the Stanhope press around 1800; about 1,100 sheets an hour for Koenig's steam press in 1814; around 2,000 sheets per feeder per hour on Hoe's type-revolving press in the 1840s; and about 14,000 complete copies an hour on a web perfecting press at the New-York Tribune by 1875. Historians also debate cause and effect. Did faster presses create mass readership, or did growing literacy, cities and advertising create a demand that pushed inventors to build faster presses? Most historians answer: both, feeding each other. Paper is a good example of a hidden bottleneck. Without the Fourdrinier machine and wood pulp, fast presses would have been starved of material, and the price of a newspaper could not have fallen to a penny. Notice too how many credits are shared or disputed in this period: Warren and Hoe for the rotary press, Robert and the Fourdriniers for the paper machine, Keller and Fenerty for wood pulp. Industrial inventions were usually the work of networks of mechanics, investors and users, not single lone geniuses.
funFact: Koenig and Bauer, the company Friedrich Koenig founded with Andreas Bauer in an old monastery near Würzburg in 1817, is still building printing presses more than 200 years later.
